title: KPMG client Westpac says trust key in audit business
full_text:
Westpac has told a parliamentary committee investigating bad behaviour at KPMG that trust in auditors is “essential to market integrity”.
Kim Lawry, the former KPMG signing partner on the Westpac account, was removed from the bank’s audit at the request of the bank. She is yet to learn whether she gets to resign from KPMG on her terms or gets sacked.
An investigation found Ms Lawry had shared a screenshot of a confidential board document, which could cost her millions of dollars in entitlements if her position is terminated. Her former boss, chief executive Andrew Yates, resigned when the audit scandal and partner misconduct first came to light, extracting a payout estimated to be about $4m.
The federal government meanwhile is understood to have extended a ban on the public service hiring KPMG by another month, to the end of October, while a review is being conducted.
The reality is that public servants are not hiring KPMG given the reputational risk of using a firm that has been found to have breached the trust of its audit clients.
KPMG auditors – whose conduct should be above reproach – were found to have misused confidential client board documents to try and win work in competitive tenders. They also promoted too-tight relationships with former KPMG partners who had joined corporate boards, and compromised their integrity by accepting free tickets to Taylor Swift and Pink concerts, as revealed by The Australian.
The matter only came to light via a whistleblower who was exited from the firm when he voiced the concerns. When Labor senator Deborah O’Neill aired his allegations under parliamentary privilege, they were initially minimised, but have proven to be true.
Ms Lawry, who was called out by the whistleblower for “bullying”, shared a screenshot of a Lendlease board scorecard during the tender process for Westpac. At that time, Lendlease and Westpac both shared Michael Ullmer (himself a former KPMG partner) as a director.
At a parliamentary joint committee hearing last month, Ms Lawry said she didn’t “recall being aware that it was confidential at the time”.
In response to questions from the committee, Westpac confirmed it requested Ms Lawry to be taken off the account “effective immediately” and made it clear that it was not her right to determine which board documents were appropriate to be shared. “Westpac agrees with the committee chair’s observation that it is irrelevant that while some may view the confidential information as not being material, the fact that it was shared is the issue.” The bank’s decision to keep KPMG as its auditor is now under review. The Australian also revealed that then-KPMG chair Martin Sheppard had hosted Westpac’s then-chair of audit Peter Nash for a sleepover.
“Peter declared his past connections with KPMG and was not on the selection committee, however he acknowledged the perception of bias that may have been created by his relationships,” Westpac wrote in its submission. The move was in breach of the bank’s policy and Mr Nash, who is also ex-KPMG, was forced to resign as a director. Mr Sheppard resigned from KPMG, along with Mr Yates, and the former head of audit Julian McPherson. Former chief operating officer Eileen Hoggett was fired and is suing KPMG. The Australian tried to reach Ms Lawry but she hung up.
